chapter: The rhythm section, family and records
title: Leroy Carr, the blues singer from Indianapolis
summary: Jones describes Leroy Carr, who kept black artists in view in the early Depression, and compares him to Jelly Roll Morton.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: Leroy Carr was the kind of a blues singer that according to our social standards at the time, from the years of '27 up to 1930, we had gone through the Bessie Smiths, the Ma Rainey, the what-have-yous, but Leroy Carr...
he came out with the blues, How Long Blues. Leroy Carr was a very fabulous guy out of Indianapolis.

Leroy died by keeping his door unlocked and everybody could come to Leroy's house to have a good time and he never got any rest. Leroy Carr when he wrote the "Prison Bound Blues", you see, he had actually been in prison and he did things with Scrapper Blackwell. He was and a very handsome man/in those periods when you had what you call race records, he was the one for 3 years to keep America and to keep the whole world alive that there were black artists, because they had forgotten about Bessie Smith, Mamie Smith, Ida Cox, and everybody including Miss Ethel Waters. But Leroy Carr was a fabulous man because had you not had Leroy Carr, the history of the other peoples going over a period of 4 or 5 years coming into Depression, when we had the TOB* and what have you - you would never known. But he was such a fabulous looking character. He was such an elite looking character. And let's I must say that he was a second edition of a Jelly Roll Morton, you see.
